src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:1:Features
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:2:================================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:4:* **scalar** and **simd** (sse, avx, neon, wasm...) optimizations
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:5:* option to use different clipspaces e.g. Left Handed, Zero-to-One... (currently right handed negative-one is default)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:6:* array api and struct api, you can use arrays or structs.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:7:* general purpose matrix operations (mat4, mat3)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:8:* chain matrix multiplication (square only)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:9:* general purpose vector operations (cross, dot, rotate, proj, angle...)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:10:* affine transformations
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:11:* matrix decomposition (extract rotation, scaling factor)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:12:* optimized affine transform matrices (mul, rigid-body inverse)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:13:* camera (lookat)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:14:* projections (ortho, perspective)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:15:* quaternions
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:16:* euler angles / yaw-pitch-roll to matrix
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:17:* extract euler angles
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:18:* inline or pre-compiled function call
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:19:* frustum (extract view frustum planes, corners...)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:20:* bounding box (AABB in Frustum (culling), crop, merge...)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:21:* 2d bounding box (crop, merge...)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:22:* bounding sphere
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:23:* project, unproject
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:24:* easing functions
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:25:* curves
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:26:* curve interpolation helpers (SMC, deCasteljau...)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:27:* helpers to convert cglm types to Apple's simd library to pass cglm types to Metal GL without packing them on both sides
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:28:* ray intersection helpers
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/features.rst:29:* and others...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:1:Array API - Inline (Default)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:2:========================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:4:This is the default API of *cglm*. All functions are forced to be inlined 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:5:and struct api, call api uses this inline api to share implementation.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:6:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:7:📌 Call api is also array api but it is not inlined. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:8:In the future there may be option to forward struct api to call api instead of inline api to reduce binary size if needed.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:9:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:10:📌 **USE this API docs for similar functions in struct and call api** 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:12:📌 In struct api you can omit namespace e.g :code:`glms_vec3_dot` can be called as :code:`vec3_dot` in struct api, see :doc:`api_struct` to configure struct api for more details.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:13:📌 In struct api functions can return struct/union
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:14:📌 In struct api you can access items like **.x**, **.y**, **.z**, **.w**, **.r**, **.g**, **.b**, **.a**, **.m00**, **m01**... 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:15:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:16:Some functions may exist twice, once for their namespace and once for global namespace
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:17:to make easier to write very common functions
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:18:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:19:For instance, in general we use :code:`glm_vec3_dot` to get dot product
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:20:of two **vec3**. Now we can also do this with :code:`glm_dot`,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:21:same for *_cross* and so on...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:22:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:23:The original function stays where it is, the function in global namespace
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:24:of same name is just an alias, so there is no call version of those functions.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:25:e.g there is no func like :code:`glmc_dot` because *glm_dot* is just alias for
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:26::code:`glm_vec3_dot`
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:27:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:28:By including **cglm/cglm.h** header you will include all inline version
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:29:of functions. Since functions in this header[s] are inline you don't need to
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:30:build or link *cglm* against your project.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:31:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:32:But by including **cglm/call.h** header you will include all *non-inline*
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:33:version of functions. You need to build *cglm* and link it.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:34:Follow the :doc:`build` documentation for this
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_inline_array.rst:35:

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:9:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:10:**Definition of aabb:**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:12:cglm defines an aabb as a two dimensional array of vec2's.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:13:The first element is the **min** point and the second one is the **max** point.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:14:If you have another type e.g. struct or even another representation then you must
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/aabb2d.rst:15:convert it before and after calling a cglm aabb2d function.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:19:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:20:    | averages the color channels into one value
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:21:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:22:    This function uses formula in COLLADA 1.5 spec which is
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:23:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:24:    .. code-block:: text
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:25:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:26:       luminance = (color.r * 0.212671) +
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:27:                   (color.g * 0.715160) +
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:28:                   (color.b * 0.072169)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:29:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:30:    It is based on the ISO/CIE color standards (see ITU-R Recommendation BT.709-4),
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:31:    that averages the color channels into one value
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/color.rst:32:

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:1:How to send vector or matrix to OpenGL like API
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:2:==================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:4:*cglm*'s vector and matrix types are arrays. So you can send them directly to a
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:5:function which accepts pointer. But you may got warnings for matrix because it is
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:6:two dimensional array.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:8:Passing / Uniforming Matrix to OpenGL:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:9:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:10:**glUniformMatrix4fv** accepts float pointer, you can pass matrix to that parameter
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:11:and it should work but with warnings. "You can pass" doesn't mean that you must pass like that.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:12:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:13:**Correct options:**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:14:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:15:Correct doesn't mean correct way to use OpenGL it is just shows correct way to pass cglm type to it.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:16:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:17:1. Pass first column
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:18:---------------------
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:19:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:20:The goal is that pass address of matrix, first element of matrix is also address of matrix,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:21:because it is array of vectors and vector is array of floats.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:22:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:23:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:24:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:25:   mat4 matrix;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:26:   /* ... */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:27:   glUniformMatrix4fv(location, 1, GL_FALSE, matrix[0]);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:28:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:29:array of matrices:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:30:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:31:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:32:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:33:   mat4 matrix;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:34:   /* ... */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:35:   glUniformMatrix4fv(location, count, GL_FALSE, matrix[0][0]);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:36:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:37:2. Cast matrix to pointer
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:38:--------------------------
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:39:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:40:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:41:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:42:   mat4 matrix;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:43:   /* ... */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:44:   glUniformMatrix4fv(location, count, GL_FALSE, (float *)matrix);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:45:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:46:in this way, passing array of matrices is same
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:47:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:48:Passing / Uniforming Vectors to OpenGL:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:49:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:50:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:51:You don't need to do extra thing when passing cglm vectors to OpengL or other APIs.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:52:Because a function like **glUniform4fv** accepts vector as pointer. cglm's vectors
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:53:are array of floats. So you can pass it directly to those functions:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:54:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:55:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:56:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:57:   vec4 vec;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:58:   /* ... */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:59:   glUniform4fv(location, 1, vec);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:60:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opengl.rst:61:this show how to pass **vec4** others are same.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:1:.. default-domain:: C
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:2:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:3:Troubleshooting
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:4:================================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:6:It is possible that you may sometimes get crashes or wrong results.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:7:Follow these topics
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:8:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:9:Memory Allocation:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:10:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:12:Recall that **cglm** does not alloc any memory on the heap.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:13:cglm functions work like memcpy; they copy data from src,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:14:make calculations, then copy the result to dest.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:15:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:16:You are responsible for allocation of **src** and **dest** parameters.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:17:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:18:Alignment:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:19:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:20:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:21:**vec4** and **mat4** types require 16 byte alignment.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:22:These types are marked with the align attribute to let the compiler know about this
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:23:requirement.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:24:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:25:Since MSVC (Windows) throws this error:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:26:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:27:**"formal parameter with requested alignment of 16 won't be aligned"**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:28:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:29:The alignment attribute has been commented out for MSVC
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:30:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:31:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:32:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:33:   #if defined(_MSC_VER)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:34:   #  define CGLM_ALIGN(X) /* __declspec(align(X)) */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:35:   #else
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:36:   #  define CGLM_ALIGN(X) __attribute((aligned(X)))
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:37:   #endif.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:38:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:39:So MSVC may not know about alignment requirements when creating variables.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:40:The interesting thing is that, if I remember correctly, Visual Studio 2017
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:41:doesn't throw the above error. So we may uncomment that line for Visual Studio 2017,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:42:you may do it yourself.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:43:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:44:**This MSVC issue is still in TODOs.**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:45:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:46:**UPDATE:** Starting with v0.4.5, cglm provides an option to disable the alignment requirement.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:47:Also, alignment is disabled for older msvc versions by default. Now alignment is only required in Visual Studio 2017 version 15.6+ if the CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED macro is not defined.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:48:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:49:Crashes, Invalid Memory Access:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:50:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:51:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:52:Most likely, you are trying to write to an invalid memory location.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:53:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:54:You may have used a wrong function for what you want to do.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:55:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:56:For example, you may have called a **glm_vec4_** function for a **vec3** data type.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:57:It will try to write 32 bytes, but since **vec3** is 24 bytes, it should throw
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:58:a memory access error or exit the app without saying anything.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:59:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:60:**UPDATE - IMPORTANT:** 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:61:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:62:  | On MSVC or some other compilers, if alignment is enabled (default) then double check alignment requirements if you got a crash.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:63:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:64:  | If you send GLM_VEC4_ONE or similar macros directly to a function, it may crash.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:65:  | Because the compiler may not apply alignment as defined on **typedef** to that macro while passing it (on stack) to a function.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:66:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:67:Wrong Results:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:68:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:69:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:70:Again, you may have used a wrong function.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:71:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:72:For instance if you use **glm_normalize()** or **glm_vec3_normalize()** for a **vec4**,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:73:it will assume that the passed param is a **vec3**, and will normalize it for **vec3**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:74:Since you need a **vec4** to be normalized in your case, you will get wrong results.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:75:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:76:Accessing a vec4 type with vec3 functions is valid, you will not get any error, exception or crash.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:77:You only get wrong results if you don't know what you are doing!
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:78:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:79:So be careful, when your IDE (Xcode, Visual Studio ...) tries to autocomplete function names, READ IT :)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:80:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:81:**Also implementation may be wrong, please let us know by creating an issue on Github.**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:82:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:83:BAD_ACCESS : Thread 1: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (code=EXC_I386_GPFLT) or Similar Errors/Crashes
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:84:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:85:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:86:This is a similar issue with alignment. For instance if you compiled **cglm** with 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:87:AVX (**-mavx**, intentionally or not) and if you use **cglm** in an environment that doesn't 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:88:support AVX (or if AVX is disabled intentionally) e.g. environment that max support SSE2/3/4, 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:89:then you probably get **BAD ACCESS** or similar...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:90:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:91:Because if you compile **cglm** with AVX it aligns **mat4** with 32 byte boundary, 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:92:and your project aligns that as a 16 byte boundary...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:93:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:94:Check alignment, supported vector extension, or simd in **cglm** and linked projects...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:95:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:96:Other Issues?
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:97:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:98:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/troubleshooting.rst:99:**Please let us know by creating an issue on Github.**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:1:.. default-domain:: C
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:2:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:3:🛠️ Options
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:4:===============================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:6:A few options are provided via macros.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:8:❗️ IMPORTANT ❗️
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:9:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:10:It's a good idea to set up your config macros in build settings like CMake, Xcode, or Visual Studio. This is especially important if you're using features like Modules in Xcode, where adding macros directly before the **cglm** headers might not work.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:12:Alignment Option
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:13:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:14:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:15:By default, **cglm** requires types to be aligned with specific byte requirements:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:16:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:17:- vec3: 8 bytes
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:18:- vec4: 16 bytes
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:19:- mat4: 16 bytes (32 on AVX)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:20:- versor: 16 bytes
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:21:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:22:Starting with **v0.4.5**, **cglm** offers an option to relax these alignment requirements. To use this option, define the **CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED** macro before including any headers. This definition can be made within Xcode, Visual Studio, other IDEs, or directly in your build system. If using pre-compiled versions of **cglm**, you'll need to compile them with the **CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED** macro.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:23:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:24:**❗️NOTE:❗️** If you're using **cglm** across multiple interdependent projects:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:25:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:26:- Always or never use the **CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED** macro in all linked projects to avoid configuration conflicts. A **cglm** header from one project could require alignment, while a header from another might not, leading to **cglm** functions accessing invalid memory locations.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:27:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:28:- **Key Point:** Maintain the same **cglm** configuration across all your projects. For example, if you activate **CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED** in one project, ensure it's set in the others too.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:29:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:30:**❗️NOTE:❗️**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:31:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:32:While **CGLM_ALL_UNALIGNED** allows for flexibility in alignment, it doesn't override C's fundamental alignment rules. For example, an array like *vec4* decays to a pointer (float*) in functions, which must adhere to the alignment requirements of a float pointer (4 bytes). This adherence is crucial because **cglm** directly dereferences these pointers instead of copying data, and failing to meet alignment requirements can lead to unpredictable errors, such as crashes.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:33:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:34:You can use `CGLM_ALIGN` and `CGLM_ALIGN_MAT` macros for aligning local variables or struct members. However, when dealing with dynamic memory allocation or custom memory locations, you'll need to ensure alignment requirements are met appropriately for those cases
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:35:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:36:Clipspace Option[s]
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:37:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:38:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:39:By starting **v0.8.3** cglm provides options to switch between clipspace configurations.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:40:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:41:Clipspace related files are located at `include/cglm/[struct]/clipspace.h` but 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:42:these are included in related files like `cam.h`. If you don't want to change your existing 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:43:clipspace configuration and want to use different clipspace function like `glm_lookat_zo` or `glm_lookat_lh_zo`...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:44:then you can include individual headers or just define `CGLM_CLIPSPACE_INCLUDE_ALL` which will include all headers for you.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:45:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:46:1. **CGLM_CLIPSPACE_INCLUDE_ALL**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:47:2. **CGLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:48:3. **CGLM_FORCE_LEFT_HANDED**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:49:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:50:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:51:1. **CGLM_CLIPSPACE_INCLUDE_ALL**:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:52:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:53:By defining this macro, **cglm** will include all clipspace functions for you by just using
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:54:`#include cglm/cglm.h` or `#include cglm/struct.h` or `#include cglm/call.h`
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:55:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:56:Otherwise you need to include header you want manually e.g. `#include cglm/clipspace/view_rh_zo.h`
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:57:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:58:2. **CGLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:59:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:60:This is similar to **GLM**'s **GLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE** option. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:61:This will set clip space between 0 to 1 which makes **cglm** Vulkan, Metal friendly. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:62:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:63:You can use functions like `glm_lookat_lh_zo()` individually. By setting **CGLM_FORCE_DEPTH_ZERO_TO_ONE**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:64:functions in cam.h for instance will use `_zo` versions.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:65:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:66:3. **CGLM_FORCE_LEFT_HANDED**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:67:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:68:Force **cglm** to use the left handed coordinate system by default, currently **cglm** uses right handed coordinate system as default,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:69:you can change this behavior with this option.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:70:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:71:**VERY VERY IMPORTANT:**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:72:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:73:Be careful if you include **cglm** in multiple projects.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:74:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:75:SSE and SSE2 Shuffle Option
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:76:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:77:**_mm_shuffle_ps** generates **shufps** instruction even if registers are same.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:78:You can force it to generate **pshufd** instruction by defining
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:79:**CGLM_NO_INT_DOMAIN** macro. As default it is not defined.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:80:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:81:SSE3 and SSE4 Dot Product Options
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:82:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:83:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:84:You have to extra options for dot product: **CGLM_SSE4_DOT** and **CGLM_SSE3_DOT**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:85:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:86:- If **SSE4** is enabled then you can define **CGLM_SSE4_DOT** to force cglm to use **_mm_dp_ps** instruction.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:87:- If **SSE3** is enabled then you can define **CGLM_SSE3_DOT** to force cglm to use **_mm_hadd_ps** instructions.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:88:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:89:otherwise cglm will use custom cglm's hadd functions which are optimized too.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:90:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:91:Struct API Options
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:92:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:93:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:94:To configure the Struct API namespace, you can define the following macros before including the cglm/struct.h header:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:95:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:96:- **CGLM_OMIT_NS_FROM_STRUCT_API**: omits CGLM_STRUCT_API_NS (`glms_`) namespace completely if there is sub namespace e.g `mat4_`, `vec4_` ... DEFAULT is not defined
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:97:- **CGLM_STRUCT_API_NS**:           define name space for struct api, DEFAULT is **glms**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:98:- **CGLM_STRUCT_API_NAME_SUFFIX**:  define name suffix, DEFAULT is **empty** e.g defining it as #define CGLM_STRUCT_API_NAME_SUFFIX  s will add s suffix to mat4_mul -> mat4s_mul
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:99:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:100:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:101:Print Options
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:102:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:103:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:104:1. **CGLM_DEFINE_PRINTS**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:105:2. **CGLM_NO_PRINTS_NOOP** (use CGLM_DEFINE_PRINTS)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:106:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:107:Inline prints are only enabled in **DEBUG** mode or if **CGLM_DEFINE_PRINTS** is defined.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:108:**glmc_** versions will always print too.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:109:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:110:Because **cglm** tried to enable print functions in debug mode and disable them in
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:111:release/production mode to eliminate printing costs when we do not need them.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:112:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:113:**cglm** checks **DEBUG** or **_DEBUG** macros to test debug mode, if these are not working for you then you can use 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:114:**CGLM_DEFINE_PRINTS** to force enable, or create a PR to introduce new macro to test against debugging mode.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:115:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:116:If DEBUG mode is not enabled then print functions will be emptied to eliminate print function calls.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:117:You can disable this feature too by defining **CGLM_DEFINE_PRINTS** macro top of cglm header 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:118:or in project/build settings...
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:119:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:120:3. **CGLM_PRINT_PRECISION**    5
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:121:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:122:precision.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:123:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:124:4. **CGLM_PRINT_MAX_TO_SHORT** 1e5
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:125:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:126:if a number is greater than this value then %g will be used, since this is shorten print you won't be able to see high precision.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:127:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:128:5. **CGLM_PRINT_COLOR**        "\033[36m"
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:129:6. **CGLM_PRINT_COLOR_RESET**  "\033[0m"
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:130:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:131:You can disable colorful print output by defining **CGLM_PRINT_COLOR** and **CGLM_PRINT_COLOR_RESET** as empty macro.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/opt.rst:132:Because some terminals may not support colors.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:6:cglm Documentation
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:7:================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:8:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:9:**cglm** is an optimized 3D math library written in C99 (compatible with C89).
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:10:It is similar to the original **glm** library, except **cglm** is mainly for
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:11:**C**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:12:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:13:**cglm** stores matrices as column-major order but in the future row-major is
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/index.rst:14:considered to be supported as optional.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:1:Build cglm
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:2:================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:4:| **cglm** does not have any external dependencies.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:6:.. note::
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:7:   If you only need to inline versions, you don't need to build **cglm**, you don't need to link it to your program.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:8:   Just import cglm to your project as dependency / external lib by copy-paste then use it as usual
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:9:

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/build.rst:23:If you don't want to install **cglm** to your system's folder you can get static and dynamic libs in this folder.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:8: **Important:** *cglm* stores quaternion as **[x, y, z, w]** in memory
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:9: since **v0.4.0** it was **[w, x, y, z]**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:10: before v0.4.0 ( **v0.3.5 and earlier** ). w is real part.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:12:What you can do with quaternions with existing functions is (Some of them):
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:13:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:14:- You can rotate transform matrix using quaternion
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:15:- You can rotate vector using quaternion
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:16:- You can create view matrix using quaternion
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/quat.rst:17:- You can create a lookrotation (from source point to dest)

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:4:====
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:6:Header: cglm/vec3.h
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:8: **Important:** *cglm* was used **glm_vec_** namespace for vec3 functions until
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:9: **v0.5.0**, since **v0.5.0** cglm uses **glm_vec3_** namespace for vec3.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:10:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:11: Also `glm_vec3_flipsign` has been renamed to `glm_vec3_negate`
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:12:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:13:We mostly use vectors in graphics math, to make writing code faster
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:14:and easy to read, some *vec3* functions are aliased in global namespace.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:15:For instance :c:func:`glm_dot` is alias of :c:func:`glm_vec3_dot`,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:16:alias means inline wrapper here. There is no call version of alias functions
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:17:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:18:There are also functions for rotating *vec3* vector. **_m4**, **_m3** prefixes
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:19:rotate *vec3* with matrix.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:539:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:540:    
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:541:    Computes refraction vector for an incident vector and a surface normal.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:542:   
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:543:    Calculates the refraction vector based on Snell's law. If total internal reflection
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:544:    occurs (angle too great given eta), dest is set to zero and returns false.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:545:    Otherwise, computes refraction vector, stores it in dest, and returns true.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:546:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:547:    Parameters:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:548:      | *[in]*  **v**     *❗️ normalized ❗️* incident vector
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:549:      | *[in]*  **n**     *❗️ normalized ❗️* normal vector
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:550:      | *[in]*  **eta**   ratio of indices of refraction (incident/transmitted)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:551:      | *[out]* **dest**  refraction vector if refraction occurs; zero vector otherwise
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:552:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:553:    Returns:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/vec3.rst:554:      returns true if refraction occurs; false if total internal reflection occurs.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:1:📚 API documentation
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:2:================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:4:**cglm** provides a few APIs for similar functions.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:6:* 📦 **Inline API**: All functions are inline. You can include **cglm/cglm.h** header
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:7:  to use this API. This is the default API. `glm_` is namespace/prefix for this API. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:8:* 📦 **Call API**: All functions are not inline. You need to build *cglm* and link it
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:9:  to your project. You can include **cglm/call.h** header to use this API. `glmc_` is namespace/prefix for this API. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:10:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:11:And also there are also sub categories:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:12:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:13:* 📦 **Array API**: Types are raw arrays and functions takes array as argument. You can include **cglm/cglm.h** header
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:14:  to use this API. This is the default API. `glm_` is namespace/prefix for this API. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:15:* 📦 **Struct API**: Types are union/struct and functions takes struct as argument and return structs if needed. You can include **cglm/struct.h** header
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:16:  to use this API. This also includes **cglm/cglm.h** header.`glms_` is namespace/prefix for this API but your can omit or change it, see struct api docs.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:17:* 📦 **SIMD API**: SIMD functions and helpers. `glmm_` is namespace/prefix for this API. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:18:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:19:📌 Since struct api and call api are built top of inline array api, follow inline array api docs for individual functions. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:20:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:21:.. toctree::
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:22:   :maxdepth: 1
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:23:   :caption: API documentations:

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:25:   api_inline_array
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:26:   api_struct
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:27:   api_call
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api.rst:28:   api_simd
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:1:.. default-domain:: C
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:2:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:3:io (input / output e.g. print)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:4:================================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:6:Header: cglm/io.h
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:8:There are some built-in print functions which may save your time,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:9:especially for debugging.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:10:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:11:All functions accept **FILE** parameter which makes very flexible.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:12:You can even print it to file on disk.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:13:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:14:In general you will want to print them to console to see results.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:15:You can use **stdout** and **stderr** to write results to console.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:16:Some programs may occupy **stdout** but you can still use **stderr**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:17:Using **stderr** is suggested.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:18:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:19:Example to print mat4 matrix:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:20:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:21:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:22:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:23:   mat4 transform;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:24:   /* ... */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:25:   glm_mat4_print(transform, stderr);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:26:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:27:.. note:: print functions use **%0.4f** precision if you need more
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:28:   (you probably will in some cases), you can change it temporary.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:29:   cglm may provide precision parameter in the future.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:32:* Now mis-alignment of columns are fixed: larger numbers are printed via %g and others are printed via %f. Column widths are calculated before print.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:33:* Now values are colorful ;)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:34:* Some print improvements
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/io.rst:35:* New options with default values:

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:1:Call API
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:2:================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:3:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:4:Call API is pre-built API for making calls from library. It is built on top of the array api. **glmc_** is the namespace for the call api. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:5:**c** stands for call. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:6:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:7:You need to built cglm to use call api. See build instructions (:doc:`build`) for more details.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:8:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:9:The functions except namespace **glmc_** are same as inline api. See ( :doc:`api_inline_array` ) for more details.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:10:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/api_call.rst:11:📌 In the future we can define option to forward inline functions or struct api to call api.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/project.rst:8:Viewport is required as *vec4* **[X, Y, Width, Height]** but this doesn't mean
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/project.rst:9:that you should store it as **vec4**. You can convert your data representation
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/project.rst:10:to vec4 before passing it to related functions.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:1:.. default-domain:: C
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:2:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:3:3D Affine Transforms
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:4:================================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:6:Header: cglm/affine.h
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:7:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:8:Before starting, **cglm** provides two kind of transform functions; pre and post. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:9:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:10:Pre functions (`T' = Tnew * T`) are like `glm_translate`, `glm_rotate` which means it will translate the vector first and then apply the model transformation.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:11:Post functions (`T' = T * Tnew`) are like `glm_translated`, `glm_rotated` which means it will apply the model transformation first and then translate the vector.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:12:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:13:`glm_translate`, `glm_rotate` are pre functions and are similar to C++ **glm** which you are familiar with. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:14:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:15:In new versions of **cglm** we added `glm_translated`, `glm_rotated`... which are post functions, 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:16:they are useful in some cases, e.g. append transform to existing transform (apply/append transform as last transform T' = T * Tnew).
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:17:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:18:Post functions are named after pre functions with `ed` suffix, e.g. `glm_translate` -> `glm_translated`. So don't mix them up.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:19:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:20:Initialize Transform Matrices
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:21:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:22:Functions with **_make** prefix expect you don't have a matrix and they create
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:23:a matrix for you. You don't need to pass identity matrix.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:24:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:25:But other functions expect you have a matrix and you want to transform them. If
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:26:you didn't have any existing matrix you have to initialize matrix to identity
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:27:before sending to transform functions.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:28:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:29:There are also functions to decompose transform matrix. These functions can't
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:30:decompose matrix after projected.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:31:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:32:Rotation Center
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:33:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:34:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:35:Rotating functions uses origin as rotation center (pivot/anchor point),
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:36:since scale factors are stored in rotation matrix, same may also true for scalling.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:37:cglm provides some functions for rotating around at given point e.g.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:38:**glm_rotate_at**, **glm_quat_rotate_at**. Use them or follow next section for algorithm ("Rotate or Scale around specific Point (Pivot Point / Anchor Point)").
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:39:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:40:Also **cglm** provides :c:func:`glm_spin` and :c:func:`glm_spinned` functions to rotate around itself. No need to give pivot.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:41:These functions are useful for rotating around center of object. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:42:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:43:Rotate or Scale around specific Point (Anchor Point)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:44:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:45:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:46:If you want to rotate model around arbitrary point follow these steps:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:47:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:48:1. Move model from pivot point to origin: **translate(-pivot.x, -pivot.y, -pivot.z)**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:49:2. Apply rotation (or scaling maybe)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:50:3. Move model back from origin to pivot (reverse of step-1): **translate(pivot.x, pivot.y, pivot.z)**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:51:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:52:**glm_rotate_at**, **glm_quat_rotate_at** and their helper functions works that way. 
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:53:So if you use them you don't need to do these steps manually which are done by **cglm**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:54:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:55:The implementation would be:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:56:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:57:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:58:  :linenos:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:59:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:60:  glm_translate(m, pivot);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:61:  glm_rotate(m, angle, axis);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:62:  glm_translate(m, pivotInv); /* pivotInv = -pivot */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:63:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:64:or just:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:65:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:66:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:67:  :linenos:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:68:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:69:  glm_rotate_at(m, pivot, angle, axis);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:70:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:71:.. _TransformsOrder:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:72:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:73:Transforms Order
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:74:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:75:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:76:It is important to understand this part especially if you call transform
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:77:functions multiple times
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:78:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:79:`glm_translate`, `glm_rotate`, `glm_scale` and `glm_quat_rotate` and their
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:80:helpers functions works like this (cglm provides reverse order as `ed` suffix e.g `glm_translated`, `glm_rotated` see post transforms):
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:81:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:82:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:83:  :linenos:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:84:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:85:  TransformMatrix = TransformMatrix * TranslateMatrix; // glm_translate()
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:86:  TransformMatrix = TransformMatrix * RotateMatrix;   // glm_rotate(), glm_quat_rotate()
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:87:  TransformMatrix = TransformMatrix * ScaleMatrix;    // glm_scale()
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:88:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:89:As you can see it is multiplied as right matrix. For instance what will happen if you call `glm_translate` twice?
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:90:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:91:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:92:  :linenos:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:93:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:94:  glm_translate(transform, translate1); /* transform = transform * translate1 */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:95:  glm_translate(transform, translate2); /* transform = transform * translate2 */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:96:  glm_rotate(transform, angle, axis)    /* transform = transform * rotation   */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:97:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:98:Now lets try to understand this:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:99:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:100:1. You call translate using `translate1` and you expect it will be first transform
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:101:because you call it first, do you?
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:102:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:103:Result will be **`transform = transform * translate1`**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:104:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:105:2. Then you call translate using `translate2` and you expect it will be second transform?
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:106:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:107:Result will be **`transform = transform * translate2`**. Now lets expand transform,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:108:it was `transform * translate1` before second call.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:109:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:110:Now it is **`transform = transform * translate1 * translate2`**, now do you understand what I say?
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:111:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:112:3. After last call transform will be:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:113:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:114:**`transform = transform * translate1 * translate2 * rotation`**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:115:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:116:The order will be; **rotation will be applied first**, then **translate2** then **translate1**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:117:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:118:It is all about matrix multiplication order. It is similar to MVP matrix:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:119:`MVP = Projection * View * Model`, model will be applied first, then view then projection.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:120:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:121:**Confused?**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:122:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:123:In the end the last function call applied first in shaders.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:124:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:125:As alternative way, you can create transform matrices individually then combine manually,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:126:but don't forget that `glm_translate`, `glm_rotate`, `glm_scale`... are optimized and should be faster (an smaller assembly output) than manual multiplication
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:127:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:128:.. code-block:: c
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:129:  :linenos:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:130:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:131:  mat4 transform1, transform2, transform3, finalTransform;
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:132:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:133:  glm_translate_make(transform1, translate1);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:134:  glm_translate_make(transform2, translate2);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:135:  glm_rotate_make(transform3, angle, axis);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:136:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:137:  /* first apply transform1, then transform2, thentransform3 */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:138:  glm_mat4_mulN((mat4 *[]){&transform3, &transform2, &transform1}, 3, finalTransform);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:139:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:140:  /* if you don't want to use mulN, same as above */
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:141:  glm_mat4_mul(transform3, transform2, finalTransform);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:142:  glm_mat4_mul(finalTransform, transform1, finalTransform);
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:143:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine.rst:144:Now transform1 will be applied first, then transform2 then transform3

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1082:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1083:    | Helper for  R (row vector) * M (matrix) * C (column vector)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1084:    |
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1085:    | **rmc** stands for **Row** * **Matrix** * **Column**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1086:    |
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1087:    | the result is scalar because M * C = ResC (1x2, column vector),
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/mat3.rst:1088:    | then if you take the dot_product(R (3x1), ResC (1x3)) = scalar value.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:2:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:3:precompiled functions (call)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:4:================================================================================
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:5:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:6:All functions in **glm_** namespace are forced to **inline**.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:7:Most functions also have pre-compiled version.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:8:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:9:Precompiled versions are in **glmc_** namespace. *c* in the namespace stands for
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:10:"call".
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:11:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:12:Since precompiled functions are just wrapper for inline versions,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:13:these functions are not documented individually.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:14:It would be duplicate documentation also it
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:15:would be hard to sync documentation between inline and call version for me.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:16:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:17:By including **clgm/cglm.h** you include all inline versions. To get precompiled
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:18:versions you need to include **cglm/call.h** header. When using the
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:19:precompiled versions, explicitly including **cglm/cglm.h** is still necessary
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/call.rst:20:for the inline versions to be included.

src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:112:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:113:    rotate existing transform matrix around given axis by angle at ORIGIN (0,0,0)
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:114:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:115:    **❗️IMPORTANT ❗️**
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:116:    
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:117:    If you need to rotate object around itself e.g. center of object or at
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:118:    some point [of object] then `glm_rotate_at()` would be better choice to do so.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:119:    
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:120:    Even if object's model transform is identity, rotation may not be around
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:121:    center of object if object does not lay out at ORIGIN perfectly.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:122:    
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:123:    Using `glm_rotate_at()` with center of bounding shape ( AABB, Sphere ... )
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:124:    would be an easy option to rotate around object if object is not at origin.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:125:    
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:126:    One another option to rotate around itself at any point is `glm_spin()`
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:127:    which is perfect if only rotating around model position is desired e.g. not
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:128:    specific point on model for instance center of geometry or center of mass,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:129:    again if geometry is not perfectly centered at origin at identity transform,
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:130:    rotation may not be around geometry.
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:131:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:132:    Parameters:
src/third_party/cglm/docs/source/affine-pre.rst:133:      | *[in, out]* **m**     affine transform

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2303:When succeeded, `*ppData` contains pointer to first byte of this memory.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2304:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2305:\warning

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2307:correctly offsetted to the beginning of region assigned to this particular allocation.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2308:Unlike the result of `vkMapMemory`, it points to the allocation, not to the beginning of the whole block.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2309:You should not add VmaAllocationInfo::offset to it!
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2310:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2311:Mapping is internally reference-counted and synchronized, so despite raw Vulkan
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2312:function `vkMapMemory()` cannot be used to map same block of `VkDeviceMemory`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2313:multiple times simultaneously, it is safe to call this function on allocations
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2314:assigned to the same memory block. Actual Vulkan memory will be mapped on first
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2315:mapping and unmapped on last unmapping.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2316:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2317:If the function succeeded, you must call vmaUnmapMemory() to unmap the
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2318:allocation when mapping is no longer needed or before freeing the allocation, at
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2319:the latest.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2320:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2321:It also safe to call this function multiple times on the same allocation. You
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2322:must call vmaUnmapMemory() same number of times as you called vmaMapMemory().
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:2323:
