src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19314:allocCreateInfo.flags = VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_DEDICATED_MEMORY_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19315:allocCreateInfo.priority = 1.0f;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19316:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19317:VkImage img;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19318:VmaAllocation alloc;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19319:vmaCreateImage(allocator, &imgCreateInfo, &allocCreateInfo, &img, &alloc, nullptr);
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19320:\endcode
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19321:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19322:<b>Also consider:</b>
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19323:Consider creating them as dedicated allocations using #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_DEDICATED_MEMORY_BIT,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19324:especially if they are large or if you plan to destroy and recreate them with different sizes
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19325:e.g. when display resolution changes.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19326:Prefer to create such resources first and all other GPU resources (like textures and vertex buffers) later.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19327:When VK_EXT_memory_priority extension is enabled, it is also worth setting high priority to such allocation
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19328:to decrease chances to be evicted to system memory by the operating system.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19329:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19330:\section usage_patterns_staging_copy_upload Staging copy for upload
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19331:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19332:<b>When:</b>
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19333:A "staging" buffer than you want to map and fill from CPU code, then use as a source of transfer
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19334:to some GPU resource.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19335:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19336:<b>What to do:</b>
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19337:Use flag #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL_WRITE_BIT.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19338:Let the library select the optimal memory type, which will always have `VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_HOST_VISIBLE_BIT`.

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19365:\section usage_patterns_readback Readback
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19366:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19367:<b>When:</b>
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19368:Buffers for data written by or transferred from the GPU that you want to read back on the CPU,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19369:e.g. results of some computations.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19370:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19371:<b>What to do:</b>
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19372:Use flag #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_RANDOM_BIT.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19373:Let the library select the optimal memory type, which will always have `VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_HOST_VISIBLE_BIT`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19374:and `VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_HOST_CACHED_BIT`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19375:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19376:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19377:VkBufferCreateInfo bufCreateInfo = { VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_BUFFER_CREATE_INFO };
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19378:bufCreateInfo.size = 65536;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19379:bufCreateInfo.usage = VK_BUFFER_USAGE_TRANSFER_DST_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19380:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19381:VmaAllocationCreateInfo allocCreateInfo = {};
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19382:allocCreateInfo.usage = VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19383:allocCreateInfo.flags = VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_RANDOM_BIT |
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19384:    VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_MAPPED_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19385:

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19395:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19396:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19397:\section usage_patterns_advanced_data_uploading Advanced data uploading
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19398:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19399:For resources that you frequently write on CPU via mapped pointer and
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19400:frequently read on GPU e.g. as a uniform buffer (also called "dynamic"), multiple options are possible:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19401:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19402:-# Easiest solution is to have one copy of the resource in `HOST_VISIBLE` memory,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19403:   even if it means system RAM (not `DEVICE_LOCAL`) on systems with a discrete graphics card,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19404:   and make the device reach out to that resource directly.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19405:   - Reads performed by the device will then go through PCI Express bus.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19406:     The performance of this access may be limited, but it may be fine depending on the size
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19407:     of this resource (whether it is small enough to quickly end up in GPU cache) and the sparsity
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19408:     of access.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19409:-# On systems with unified memory (e.g. AMD APU or Intel integrated graphics, mobile chips),
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19410:   a memory type may be available that is both `HOST_VISIBLE` (available for mapping) and `DEVICE_LOCAL`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19411:   (fast to access from the GPU). Then, it is likely the best choice for such type of resource.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19412:-# Systems with a discrete graphics card and separate video memory may or may not expose
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19413:   a memory type that is both `HOST_VISIBLE` and `DEVICE_LOCAL`, also known as Base Address Register (BAR).
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19414:   If they do, it represents a piece of VRAM (or entire VRAM, if ReBAR is enabled in the motherboard BIOS)
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19415:   that is available to CPU for mapping.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19416:   - Writes performed by the host to that memory go through PCI Express bus.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19417:     The performance of these writes may be limited, but it may be fine, especially on PCIe 4.0,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19418:     as long as rules of using uncached and write-combined memory are followed - only sequential writes and no reads.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19419:-# Finally, you may need or prefer to create a separate copy of the resource in `DEVICE_LOCAL` memory,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19420:   a separate "staging" copy in `HOST_VISIBLE` memory and perform an explicit transfer command between them.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19421:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19422:Thankfully, VMA offers an aid to create and use such resources in the the way optimal
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19423:for the current Vulkan device. To help the library make the best choice,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19424:use flag #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL_WRITE_BIT together with
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19425:#VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_ALLOW_TRANSFER_INSTEAD_BIT.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19426:It will then prefer a memory type that is both `DEVICE_LOCAL` and `HOST_VISIBLE` (integrated memory or BAR),
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19427:but if no such memory type is available or allocation from it fails
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19428:(PC graphics cards have only 256 MB of BAR by default, unless ReBAR is supported and enabled in BIOS),
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19429:it will fall back to `DEVICE_LOCAL` memory for fast GPU access.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19430:It is then up to you to detect that the allocation ended up in a memory type that is not `HOST_VISIBLE`,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19431:so you need to create another "staging" allocation and perform explicit transfers.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19432:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19433:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19434:VkBufferCreateInfo bufCreateInfo = { VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_BUFFER_CREATE_INFO };
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19435:bufCreateInfo.size = 65536;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19436:bufCreateInfo.usage = VK_BUFFER_USAGE_UNIFORM_BUFFER_BIT | VK_BUFFER_USAGE_TRANSFER_DST_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19437:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19438:VmaAllocationCreateInfo allocCreateInfo = {};

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19440:allocCreateInfo.flags = VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL_WRITE_BIT |
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19441:    VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_ALLOW_TRANSFER_INSTEAD_BIT |
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19442:    VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_MAPPED_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19443:

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19532:\section usage_patterns_other_use_cases Other use cases
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19533:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19534:Here are some other, less obvious use cases and their recommended settings:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19535:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19536:- An image that is used only as transfer source and destination, but it should stay on the device,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19537:  as it is used to temporarily store a copy of some texture, e.g. from the current to the next frame,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19538:  for temporal antialiasing or other temporal effects.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19539:  - Use `VkImageCreateInfo::usage = VK_IMAGE_USAGE_TRANSFER_SRC_BIT | VK_IMAGE_USAGE_TRANSFER_DST_BIT`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19540:  - Use VmaAllocationCreateInfo::usage = #VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19541:- An image that is used only as transfer source and destination, but it should be placed
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19542:  in the system RAM despite it doesn't need to be mapped, because it serves as a "swap" copy to evict
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19543:  least recently used textures from VRAM.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19544:  - Use `VkImageCreateInfo::usage = VK_IMAGE_USAGE_TRANSFER_SRC_BIT | VK_IMAGE_USAGE_TRANSFER_DST_BIT`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19545:  - Use VmaAllocationCreateInfo::usage = #VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO_PREFER_HOST,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19546:    as VMA needs a hint here to differentiate from the previous case.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19547:- A buffer that you want to map and write from the CPU, directly read from the GPU
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19548:  (e.g. as a uniform or vertex buffer), but you have a clear preference to place it in device or
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19549:  host memory due to its large size.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19550:  - Use `VkBufferCreateInfo::usage = VK_BUFFER_USAGE_UNIFORM_BUFFER_BIT`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19551:  - Use VmaAllocationCreateInfo::usage = #VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO_PREFER_DEVICE or #VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO_PREFER_HOST
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19552:  - Use VmaAllocationCreateInfo::flags = #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_HOST_ACCESS_SEQUENTIAL_WRITE_BIT
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19553:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19554:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19555:\page configuration Configuration
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19556:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19557:Please check "CONFIGURATION SECTION" in the code to find macros that you can define
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19558:before each include of this file or change directly in this file to provide
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19559:your own implementation of basic facilities like assert, `min()` and `max()` functions,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19560:mutex, atomic etc.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19561:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19562:For example, define `VMA_ASSERT(expr)` before including the library to provide
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19563:custom implementation of the assertion, compatible with your project.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19564:By default it is defined to standard C `assert(expr)` in `_DEBUG` configuration
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19565:and empty otherwise.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19566:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19567:Similarly, you can define `VMA_LEAK_LOG_FORMAT` macro to enable printing of leaked (unfreed) allocations,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19568:including their names and other parameters. Example:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19569:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19570:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19571:#define VMA_LEAK_LOG_FORMAT(format, ...) do { \
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19572:        printf((format), __VA_ARGS__); \
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19573:        printf("\n"); \
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19574:    } while(false)
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19575:\endcode
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19576:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19577:\section config_Vulkan_functions Pointers to Vulkan functions
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19578:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19579:There are multiple ways to import pointers to Vulkan functions in the library.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19580:In the simplest case you don't need to do anything.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19581:If the compilation or linking of your program or the initialization of the #VmaAllocator
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19582:doesn't work for you, you can try to reconfigure it.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19583:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19584:First, the allocator tries to fetch pointers to Vulkan functions linked statically,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19585:like this:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19586:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19587:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19588:m_VulkanFunctions.vkAllocateMemory = (PFN_vkAllocateMemory)vkAllocateMemory;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19589:\endcode
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19590:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19591:If you want to disable this feature, set configuration macro: `#define VMA_STATIC_VULKAN_FUNCTIONS 0`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19592:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19593:Second, you can provide the pointers yourself by setting member VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::pVulkanFunctions.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19594:You can fetch them e.g. using functions `vkGetInstanceProcAddr` and `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` or
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19595:by using a helper library like [volk](https://github.com/zeux/volk).
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19596:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19597:Third, VMA tries to fetch remaining pointers that are still null by calling
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19598:`vkGetInstanceProcAddr` and `vkGetDeviceProcAddr` on its own.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19599:You need to only fill in VmaVulkanFunctions::vkGetInstanceProcAddr and VmaVulkanFunctions::vkGetDeviceProcAddr.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19600:Other pointers will be fetched automatically.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19601:If you want to disable this feature, set configuration macro: `#define VMA_DYNAMIC_VULKAN_FUNCTIONS 0`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19602:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19603:Finally, all the function pointers required by the library (considering selected
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19604:Vulkan version and enabled extensions) are checked with `VMA_ASSERT` if they are not null.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19605:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19606:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19607:\section custom_memory_allocator Custom host memory allocator
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19608:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19609:If you use custom allocator for CPU memory rather than default operator `new`
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19610:and `delete` from C++, you can make this library using your allocator as well
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19611:by filling optional member VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::pAllocationCallbacks. These
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19612:functions will be passed to Vulkan, as well as used by the library itself to
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19613:make any CPU-side allocations.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19614:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19615:\section allocation_callbacks Device memory allocation callbacks
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19616:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19617:The library makes calls to `vkAllocateMemory()` and `vkFreeMemory()` internally.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19618:You can setup callbacks to be informed about these calls, e.g. for the purpose
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19619:of gathering some statistics. To do it, fill optional member
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19620:VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::pDeviceMemoryCallbacks.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19621:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19622:\section heap_memory_limit Device heap memory limit
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19623:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19624:When device memory of certain heap runs out of free space, new allocations may
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19625:fail (returning error code) or they may succeed, silently pushing some existing_
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19626:memory blocks from GPU VRAM to system RAM (which degrades performance). This
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19627:behavior is implementation-dependent - it depends on GPU vendor and graphics
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19628:driver.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19629:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19630:On AMD cards it can be controlled while creating Vulkan device object by using
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19631:VK_AMD_memory_overallocation_behavior extension, if available.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19632:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19633:Alternatively, if you want to test how your program behaves with limited amount of Vulkan device
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19634:memory available without switching your graphics card to one that really has
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19635:smaller VRAM, you can use a feature of this library intended for this purpose.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19636:To do it, fill optional member VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::pHeapSizeLimit.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19637:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19638:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19639:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19640:\page vk_khr_dedicated_allocation VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19641:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19642:VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation is a Vulkan extension which can be used to improve
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19643:performance on some GPUs. It augments Vulkan API with possibility to query
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19644:driver whether it prefers particular buffer or image to have its own, dedicated
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19645:allocation (separate `VkDeviceMemory` block) for better efficiency - to be able
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19646:to do some internal optimizations. The extension is supported by this library.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19647:It will be used automatically when enabled.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19648:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19649:It has been promoted to core Vulkan 1.1, so if you use eligible Vulkan version
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19650:and inform VMA about it by setting VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::vulkanApiVersion,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19651:you are all set.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19652:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19653:Otherwise, if you want to use it as an extension:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19654:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19655:1 . When creating Vulkan device, check if following 2 device extensions are
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19656:supported (call `vkEnumerateDeviceExtensionProperties()`).
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19657:If yes, enable them (fill `VkDeviceCreateInfo::ppEnabledExtensionNames`).
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19658:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19659:- VK_KHR_get_memory_requirements2
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19660:- VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19661:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19662:If you enabled these extensions:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19663:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19664:2 . Use #VMA_ALLOCATOR_CREATE_KHR_DEDICATED_ALLOCATION_BIT flag when creating
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19665:your #VmaAllocator to inform the library that you enabled required extensions
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19666:and you want the library to use them.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19667:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19668:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19669:allocatorInfo.flags |= VMA_ALLOCATOR_CREATE_KHR_DEDICATED_ALLOCATION_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19670:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19671:vmaCreateAllocator(&allocatorInfo, &allocator);
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19672:\endcode
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19673:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19674:That is all. The extension will be automatically used whenever you create a
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19675:buffer using vmaCreateBuffer() or image using vmaCreateImage().
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19676:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19677:When using the extension together with Vulkan Validation Layer, you will receive
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19678:warnings like this:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19679:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19680:_vkBindBufferMemory(): Binding memory to buffer 0x33 but vkGetBufferMemoryRequirements() has not been called on that buffer._
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19681:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19682:It is OK, you should just ignore it. It happens because you use function
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19683:`vkGetBufferMemoryRequirements2KHR()` instead of standard
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19684:`vkGetBufferMemoryRequirements()`, while the validation layer seems to be
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19685:unaware of it.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19686:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19687:To learn more about this extension, see:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19688:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19689:- [VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation in Vulkan specification](https://www.khronos.org/registry/vulkan/specs/1.2-extensions/html/chap50.html#VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation)
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19690:- [VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation unofficial manual](http://asawicki.info/articles/VK_KHR_dedicated_allocation.php5)
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19691:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19692:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19693:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19694:\page vk_ext_memory_priority VK_EXT_memory_priority
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19695:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19696:VK_EXT_memory_priority is a device extension that allows to pass additional "priority"
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19697:value to Vulkan memory allocations that the implementation may use prefer certain
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19698:buffers and images that are critical for performance to stay in device-local memory
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19699:in cases when the memory is over-subscribed, while some others may be moved to the system memory.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19700:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19701:VMA offers convenient usage of this extension.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19702:If you enable it, you can pass "priority" parameter when creating allocations or custom pools
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19703:and the library automatically passes the value to Vulkan using this extension.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19704:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19705:If you want to use this extension in connection with VMA, follow these steps:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19706:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19707:\section vk_ext_memory_priority_initialization Initialization
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19708:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19709:1) Call `vkEnumerateDeviceExtensionProperties` for the physical device.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19710:Check if the extension is supported - if returned array of `VkExtensionProperties` contains "VK_EXT_memory_priority".
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19711:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19712:2) Call `vkGetPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` for the physical device instead of old `vkGetPhysicalDeviceFeatures`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19713:Attach additional structure `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryPriorityFeaturesEXT` to `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2::pNext` to be returned.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19714:Check if the device feature is really supported - check if `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryPriorityFeaturesEXT::memoryPriority` is true.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19715:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19716:3) While creating device with `vkCreateDevice`, enable this extension - add "VK_EXT_memory_priority"
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19717:to the list passed as `VkDeviceCreateInfo::ppEnabledExtensionNames`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19718:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19719:4) While creating the device, also don't set `VkDeviceCreateInfo::pEnabledFeatures`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19720:Fill in `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` structure instead and pass it as `VkDeviceCreateInfo::pNext`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19721:Enable this device feature - attach additional structure `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryPriorityFeaturesEXT` to
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19722:`VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2::pNext` chain and set its member `memoryPriority` to `VK_TRUE`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19723:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19724:5) While creating #VmaAllocator with vmaCreateAllocator() inform VMA that you
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19725:have enabled this extension and feature - add #VMA_ALLOCATOR_CREATE_EXT_MEMORY_PRIORITY_BIT
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19726:to VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::flags.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19727:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19728:\section vk_ext_memory_priority_usage Usage
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19729:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19730:When using this extension, you should initialize following member:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19731:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19732:- VmaAllocationCreateInfo::priority when creating a dedicated allocation with #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_DEDICATED_MEMORY_BIT.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19733:- VmaPoolCreateInfo::priority when creating a custom pool.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19734:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19735:It should be a floating-point value between `0.0f` and `1.0f`, where recommended default is `0.5F`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19736:Memory allocated with higher value can be treated by the Vulkan implementation as higher priority
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19737:and so it can have lower chances of being pushed out to system memory, experiencing degraded performance.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19738:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19739:It might be a good idea to create performance-critical resources like color-attachment or depth-stencil images
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19740:as dedicated and set high priority to them. For example:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19741:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19742:\code
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19743:VkImageCreateInfo imgCreateInfo = { VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_IMAGE_CREATE_INFO };
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19744:imgCreateInfo.imageType = VK_IMAGE_TYPE_2D;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19745:imgCreateInfo.extent.width = 3840;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19746:imgCreateInfo.extent.height = 2160;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19747:imgCreateInfo.extent.depth = 1;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19748:imgCreateInfo.mipLevels = 1;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19749:imgCreateInfo.arrayLayers = 1;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19750:imgCreateInfo.format = VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19751:imgCreateInfo.tiling = VK_IMAGE_TILING_OPTIMAL;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19752:imgCreateInfo.initialLayout = VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_UNDEFINED;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19753:imgCreateInfo.usage = VK_IMAGE_USAGE_SAMPLED_BIT | VK_IMAGE_USAGE_COLOR_ATTACHMENT_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19754:imgCreateInfo.samples = VK_SAMPLE_COUNT_1_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19755:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19756:VmaAllocationCreateInfo allocCreateInfo = {};
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19757:allocCreateInfo.usage = VMA_MEMORY_USAGE_AUTO;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19758:allocCreateInfo.flags = VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_DEDICATED_MEMORY_BIT;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19759:allocCreateInfo.priority = 1.0f;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19760:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19761:VkImage img;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19762:VmaAllocation alloc;
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19763:vmaCreateImage(allocator, &imgCreateInfo, &allocCreateInfo, &img, &alloc, nullptr);
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19764:\endcode
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19765:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19766:`priority` member is ignored in the following situations:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19767:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19768:- Allocations created in custom pools: They inherit the priority, along with all other allocation parameters
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19769:  from the parameters passed in #VmaPoolCreateInfo when the pool was created.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19770:- Allocations created in default pools: They inherit the priority from the parameters
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19771:  VMA used when creating default pools, which means `priority == 0.5F`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19772:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19773:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19774:\page vk_amd_device_coherent_memory VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19775:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19776:VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory is a device extension that enables access to
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19777:additional memory types with `VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_DEVICE_COHERENT_BIT_AMD` and
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19778:`VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_DEVICE_UNCACHED_BIT_AMD` flag. It is useful mostly for
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19779:allocation of buffers intended for writing "breadcrumb markers" in between passes
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19780:or draw calls, which in turn are useful for debugging GPU crash/hang/TDR cases.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19781:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19782:When the extension is available but has not been enabled, Vulkan physical device
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19783:still exposes those memory types, but their usage is forbidden. VMA automatically
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19784:takes care of that - it returns `VK_ERROR_FEATURE_NOT_PRESENT` when an attempt
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19785:to allocate memory of such type is made.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19786:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19787:If you want to use this extension in connection with VMA, follow these steps:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19788:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19789:\section vk_amd_device_coherent_memory_initialization Initialization
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19790:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19791:1) Call `vkEnumerateDeviceExtensionProperties` for the physical device.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19792:Check if the extension is supported - if returned array of `VkExtensionProperties` contains "VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory".
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19793:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19794:2) Call `vkGetPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` for the physical device instead of old `vkGetPhysicalDeviceFeatures`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19795:Attach additional structure `VkPhysicalDeviceCoherentMemoryFeaturesAMD` to `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2::pNext` to be returned.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19796:Check if the device feature is really supported - check if `VkPhysicalDeviceCoherentMemoryFeaturesAMD::deviceCoherentMemory` is true.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19797:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19798:3) While creating device with `vkCreateDevice`, enable this extension - add "VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory"
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19799:to the list passed as `VkDeviceCreateInfo::ppEnabledExtensionNames`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19800:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19801:4) While creating the device, also don't set `VkDeviceCreateInfo::pEnabledFeatures`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19802:Fill in `VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2` structure instead and pass it as `VkDeviceCreateInfo::pNext`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19803:Enable this device feature - attach additional structure `VkPhysicalDeviceCoherentMemoryFeaturesAMD` to
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19804:`VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2::pNext` and set its member `deviceCoherentMemory` to `VK_TRUE`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19805:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19806:5) While creating #VmaAllocator with vmaCreateAllocator() inform VMA that you
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19807:have enabled this extension and feature - add #VMA_ALLOCATOR_CREATE_AMD_DEVICE_COHERENT_MEMORY_BIT
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19808:to VmaAllocatorCreateInfo::flags.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19809:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19810:\section vk_amd_device_coherent_memory_usage Usage
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19811:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19812:After following steps described above, you can create VMA allocations and custom pools
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19813:out of the special `DEVICE_COHERENT` and `DEVICE_UNCACHED` memory types on eligible
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19814:devices. There are multiple ways to do it, for example:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19815:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19816:- You can request or prefer to allocate out of such memory types by adding
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19817:  `VK_MEMORY_PROPERTY_DEVICE_UNCACHED_BIT_AMD` to VmaAllocationCreateInfo::requiredFlags
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19818:  or VmaAllocationCreateInfo::preferredFlags. Those flags can be freely mixed with
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19819:  other ways of \ref choosing_memory_type, like setting VmaAllocationCreateInfo::usage.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19820:- If you manually found memory type index to use for this purpose, force allocation
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19821:  from this specific index by setting VmaAllocationCreateInfo::memoryTypeBits `= 1U << index`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19822:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19823:\section vk_amd_device_coherent_memory_more_information More information
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19824:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19825:To learn more about this extension, see [VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory in Vulkan specification](https://www.khronos.org/registry/vulkan/specs/1.2-extensions/man/html/VK_AMD_device_coherent_memory.html)
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19826:

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19860:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19861:\section enabling_buffer_device_address_usage Usage
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19862:

src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19879:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19880:\section general_considerations_thread_safety Thread safety
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19881:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19882:- The library has no global state, so separate #VmaAllocator objects can be used
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19883:  independently.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19884:  There should be no need to create multiple such objects though - one per `VkDevice` is enough.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19885:- By default, all calls to functions that take #VmaAllocator as first parameter
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19886:  are safe to call from multiple threads simultaneously because they are
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19887:  synchronized internally when needed.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19888:  This includes allocation and deallocation from default memory pool, as well as custom #VmaPool.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19889:- When the allocator is created with #VMA_ALLOCATOR_CREATE_EXTERNALLY_SYNCHRONIZED_BIT
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19890:  flag, calls to functions that take such #VmaAllocator object must be
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19891:  synchronized externally.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19892:- Access to a #VmaAllocation object must be externally synchronized. For example,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19893:  you must not call vmaGetAllocationInfo() and vmaMapMemory() from different
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19894:  threads at the same time if you pass the same #VmaAllocation object to these
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19895:  functions.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19896:- #VmaVirtualBlock is not safe to be used from multiple threads simultaneously.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19897:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19898:\section general_considerations_versioning_and_compatibility Versioning and compatibility
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19899:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19900:The library uses [**Semantic Versioning**](https://semver.org/),
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19901:which means version numbers follow convention: Major.Minor.Patch (e.g. 2.3.0), where:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19902:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19903:- Incremented Patch version means a release is backward- and forward-compatible,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19904:  introducing only some internal improvements, bug fixes, optimizations etc.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19905:  or changes that are out of scope of the official API described in this documentation.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19906:- Incremented Minor version means a release is backward-compatible,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19907:  so existing code that uses the library should continue to work, while some new
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19908:  symbols could have been added: new structures, functions, new values in existing
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19909:  enums and bit flags, new structure members, but not new function parameters.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19910:- Incrementing Major version means a release could break some backward compatibility.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19911:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19912:All changes between official releases are documented in file "CHANGELOG.md".
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19913:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19914:\warning Backward compatibility is considered on the level of C++ source code, not binary linkage.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19915:Adding new members to existing structures is treated as backward compatible if initializing
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19916:the new members to binary zero results in the old behavior.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19917:You should always fully initialize all library structures to zeros and not rely on their
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19918:exact binary size.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19919:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19920:\section general_considerations_validation_layer_warnings Validation layer warnings
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19921:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19922:When using this library, you can meet following types of warnings issued by
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19923:Vulkan validation layer. They don't necessarily indicate a bug, so you may need
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19924:to just ignore them.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19925:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19926:- *Mapping an image with layout VK_IMAGE_LAYOUT_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_OPTIMAL can result in undefined behavior if this memory is used by the device. Only GENERAL or PREINITIALIZED should be used.*
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19927:  - It happens when you map a buffer or image, because the library maps entire
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19928:    `VkDeviceMemory` block, where different types of images and buffers may end
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19929:    up together, especially on GPUs with unified memory like Intel.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19930:- *Non-linear image 0xebc91 is aliased with linear buffer 0xeb8e4 which may indicate a bug.*
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19931:  - It may happen when you use [defragmentation](@ref defragmentation).
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19932:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19933:\section general_considerations_allocation_algorithm Allocation algorithm
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19934:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19935:The library uses following algorithm for allocation, in order:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19936:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19937:-# Try to find free range of memory in existing blocks.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19938:-# If failed, try to create a new block of `VkDeviceMemory`, with preferred block size.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19939:-# If failed, try to create such block with size / 2, size / 4, size / 8.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19940:-# If failed, try to allocate separate `VkDeviceMemory` for this allocation,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19941:   just like when you use #VMA_ALLOCATION_CREATE_DEDICATED_MEMORY_BIT.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19942:-# If failed, choose other memory type that meets the requirements specified in
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19943:   VmaAllocationCreateInfo and go to point 1.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19944:-# If failed, return `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY`.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19945:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19946:\section general_considerations_features_not_supported Features not supported
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19947:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19948:Features deliberately excluded from the scope of this library:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19949:
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19950:-# **Data transfer.** Uploading (streaming) and downloading data of buffers and images
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19951:   between CPU and GPU memory and related synchronization is responsibility of the user.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19952:   Defining some "texture" object that would automatically stream its data from a
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19953:   staging copy in CPU memory to GPU memory would rather be a feature of another,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19954:   higher-level library implemented on top of VMA.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19955:   VMA doesn't record any commands to a `VkCommandBuffer`. It just allocates memory.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19956:-# **Recreation of buffers and images.** Although the library has functions for
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19957:   buffer and image creation: vmaCreateBuffer(), vmaCreateImage(), you need to
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19958:   recreate these objects yourself after defragmentation. That is because the big
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19959:   structures `VkBufferCreateInfo`, `VkImageCreateInfo` are not stored in
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19960:   #VmaAllocation object.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19961:-# **Handling CPU memory allocation failures.** When dynamically creating small C++
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19962:   objects in CPU memory (not Vulkan memory), allocation failures are not checked
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19963:   and handled gracefully, because that would complicate code significantly and
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19964:   is usually not needed in desktop PC applications anyway.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19965:   Success of an allocation is just checked with an assert.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19966:-# **Code free of any compiler warnings.** Maintaining the library to compile and
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19967:   work correctly on so many different platforms is hard enough. Being free of
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19968:   any warnings, on any version of any compiler, is simply not feasible.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19969:   There are many preprocessor macros that make some variables unused, function parameters unreferenced,
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19970:   or conditional expressions constant in some configurations.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19971:   The code of this library should not be bigger or more complicated just to silence these warnings.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19972:   It is recommended to disable such warnings instead.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19973:-# This is a C++ library with C interface. **Bindings or ports to any other programming languages** are welcome as external projects but
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19974:   are not going to be included into this repository.
src/third_party/vk_mem_alloc.h:19975:*/

src/third_party/volk/README.md:2:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:3:## Purpose
src/third_party/volk/README.md:4:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:5:volk is a meta-loader for Vulkan. It allows you to dynamically load entrypoints required to use Vulkan
src/third_party/volk/README.md:6:without linking to vulkan-1.dll or statically linking Vulkan loader. Additionally, volk simplifies the use of Vulkan extensions by automatically loading all associated entrypoints. Finally, volk enables loading
src/third_party/volk/README.md:7:Vulkan entrypoints directly from the driver which can increase performance by skipping loader dispatch overhead.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:8:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:9:volk is written in C89 and supports Windows, Linux, Android and macOS (via MoltenVK).
src/third_party/volk/README.md:10:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:11:## Building
src/third_party/volk/README.md:12:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:13:There are multiple ways to use volk in your project:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:14:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:15:1. You can add `volk.c` to your build system. Note that the usual preprocessor defines that enable Vulkan's platform-specific functions (VK_USE_PLATFORM_WIN32_KHR, VK_USE_PLATFORM_XLIB_KHR, VK_USE_PLATFORM_MACOS_MVK, etc) must be passed as desired to the compiler when building `volk.c`.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:16:2. You can use provided CMake files, with the usage detailed below.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:17:3. You can use volk in header-only fashion. Include `volk.h` wherever you want to use Vulkan functions. In exactly one source file, define `VOLK_IMPLEMENTATION` before including `volk.h`. Do not build `volk.c` at all in this case - however, `volk.c` must still be in the same directory as `volk.h`. This method of integrating volk makes it possible to set the platform defines mentioned above with arbitrary (preprocessor) logic in your code.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:18:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:19:## Basic usage
src/third_party/volk/README.md:20:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:21:To use volk, you have to include `volk.h` instead of `vulkan/vulkan.h`; this is necessary to use function definitions from volk.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:22:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:23:If some files in your application include `vulkan/vulkan.h` and don't include `volk.h`, this can result in symbol conflicts; consider defining `VK_NO_PROTOTYPES` when compiling code that uses Vulkan to make sure this doesn't happen. It's also important to make sure that `vulkan-1` is not linked into the application, as this results in symbol name conflicts as well.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:24:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:25:To initialize volk, call this function first:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:26:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:27:```c++
src/third_party/volk/README.md:28:VkResult volkInitialize();
src/third_party/volk/README.md:29:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:30:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:31:This will attempt to load Vulkan loader from the system; if this function returns `VK_SUCCESS` you can proceed to create Vulkan instance.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:32:If this function fails, this means Vulkan loader isn't installed on your system.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:33:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:34:After creating the Vulkan instance using Vulkan API, call this function:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:35:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:36:```c++
src/third_party/volk/README.md:37:void volkLoadInstance(VkInstance instance);
src/third_party/volk/README.md:38:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:39:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:40:This function will load all required Vulkan entrypoints, including all extensions; you can use Vulkan from here on as usual.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:41:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:42:## Optimizing device calls
src/third_party/volk/README.md:43:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:44:If you use volk as described in the previous section, all device-related function calls, such as `vkCmdDraw`, will go through Vulkan loader dispatch code.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:45:This allows you to transparently support multiple VkDevice objects in the same application, but comes at a price of dispatch overhead which can be as high as 7% depending on the driver and application.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:46:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:47:To avoid this, you have two options:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:48:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:49:1. For applications that use just one VkDevice object, load device-related Vulkan entrypoints directly from the driver with this function:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:50:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:51:```c++
src/third_party/volk/README.md:52:void volkLoadDevice(VkDevice device);
src/third_party/volk/README.md:53:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:54:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:55:2. For applications that use multiple VkDevice objects, load device-related Vulkan entrypoints into a table:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:56:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:57:```c++
src/third_party/volk/README.md:58:void volkLoadDeviceTable(struct VolkDeviceTable* table, VkDevice device);
src/third_party/volk/README.md:59:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:60:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:61:The second option requires you to change the application code to store one `VolkDeviceTable` per `VkDevice` and call functions from this table instead.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:62:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:63:Device entrypoints are loaded using `vkGetDeviceProcAddr`; when no layers are present, this commonly results in most function pointers pointing directly at the driver functions, minimizing the call overhead. When layers are loaded, the entrypoints will point at the implementations in the first applicable layer, so this is compatible with any layers including validation layers.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:64:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:65:Since `volkLoadDevice` overwrites some function pointers with device-specific versions, you can choose to use `volkLoadInstanceOnly` instead of `volkLoadInstance`; when using table-based interface this can also help enforce the usage of the function tables as `volkLoadInstanceOnly` will leave device-specific functions as `NULL`.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:66:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:67:## CMake support
src/third_party/volk/README.md:68:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:69:If your project uses CMake, volk provides you with targets corresponding to the different use cases:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:70:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:71:1. Target `volk` is a static library. Any platform defines can be passed to the compiler by setting `VOLK_STATIC_DEFINES`. Example:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:72:```cmake
src/third_party/volk/README.md:73:if (WIN32)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:74:   set(VOLK_STATIC_DEFINES VK_USE_PLATFORM_WIN32_KHR)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:75:elseif()
src/third_party/volk/README.md:76:   ...
src/third_party/volk/README.md:77:endif()
src/third_party/volk/README.md:78:add_subdirectory(volk)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:79:target_link_library(my_application PRIVATE volk)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:80:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:81:2. Target `volk_headers` is an interface target for the header-only style. Example:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:82:```cmake
src/third_party/volk/README.md:83:add_subdirectory(volk)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:84:target_link_library(my_application PRIVATE volk_headers)
src/third_party/volk/README.md:85:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:86:and in the code:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:87:```c
src/third_party/volk/README.md:88:/* ...any logic setting VK_USE_PLATFORM_WIN32_KHR and friends... */
src/third_party/volk/README.md:89:#define VOLK_IMPLEMENTATION
src/third_party/volk/README.md:90:#include "volk.h"
src/third_party/volk/README.md:91:```
src/third_party/volk/README.md:92:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:93:The above example use `add_subdirectory` to include volk into CMake's build tree. This is a good choice if you copy the volk files into your project tree or as a git submodule.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:94:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:95:volk also supports installation and config-file packages. Installation is disabled by default (so as to not pollute user projects with install rules), and can be enabled by passing `-DVOLK_INSTALL=ON` to CMake. Once installed, do something like `find_package(volk CONFIG REQUIRED)` in your project's CMakeLists.txt. The imported volk targets are called `volk::volk` and `volk::volk_headers`.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:96:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:97:## Configuration
src/third_party/volk/README.md:98:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:99:By default, volk is compiled as a C library and exposes all Vulkan function pointers as globals. This can result in symbol conflicts if some libraries in the application are still linking to Vulkan libraries directly. While generally speaking it's desirable to not mix & match volk with direct usage of Vulkan - for example, mixed usage means the application still links directly to Vulkan libraries and will fail to launch if Vulkan is not available on the user's system - it's possible to enable `VOLK_NAMESPACE` CMake option (or `VOLK_NAMESPACE` define when building volk manually), which places all volk symbols into `volk::` namespace. This requires compiling `volk.c` in C++ mode, which happens automatically when using CMake, but doesn't require any other changes.
src/third_party/volk/README.md:100:
src/third_party/volk/README.md:101:Device level functions can be hidden by defining `VOLK_NO_DEVICE_PROTOTYPES`. When using `volkLoadInstanceOnly` and `volkLoadDeviceTable` the device level functions are never loaded and when not used correctly would trigger a runtime error. By hiding the device prototypes mistakes can be checked by the compiler.

src/net_channel.c:16:static bool net_seqnum_in_window(uint16_t seqnum, uint16_t next, uint16_t window_size) {
src/net_channel.c:17:    uint16_t window_start = next;
src/net_channel.c:18:    uint16_t window_end = (uint16_t)((next + window_size) % (NET_SEQNUM_MAX + 1));

src/net_channel.c:154:static void net_channel_push_ready_owned(NetChannel *ch, uint8_t *owned_data, size_t len) {
src/net_channel.c:155:    NetReadyNode *node = malloc(sizeof(NetReadyNode));

src/net_channel.c:163:

src/net_channel.c:165:        ch->ready_tail->next = node;
src/net_channel.c:166:    else
src/net_channel.c:167:        ch->ready_head = node;
src/net_channel.c:168:    ch->ready_tail = node;
src/net_channel.c:169:}
src/net_channel.c:170:
src/net_channel.c:171:/* Copies `data` into a fresh heap allocation and pushes it, for the common
src/net_channel.c:172: * case (ORIGINAL payloads) where the source isn't already something we can
src/net_channel.c:173: * hand off ownership of directly. */
src/net_channel.c:174:static void net_channel_push_ready_copy(NetChannel *ch, const uint8_t *data, size_t len) {
src/net_channel.c:175:    uint8_t *owned = malloc(len > 0 ? len : 1);
src/net_channel.c:176:    if (!owned) {
src/net_channel.c:177:        fprintf(stderr, "net_channel: OOM allocating %zu-byte ready payload\n", len);
src/net_channel.c:178:        exit(1);
src/net_channel.c:179:    }
src/net_channel.c:180:    memcpy(owned, data, len);
src/net_channel.c:181:    net_channel_push_ready_owned(ch, owned, len);
src/net_channel.c:182:}

src/world.c:5:// Bit-mixer (murmur3-style finalizer): avalanches a single 32-bit value so
src/world.c:6:// small input changes flip roughly half the output bits. Casting the
src/world.c:7:// signed ChunkCoord fields to uint32_t before this runs sidesteps
src/world.c:8:// implementation-defined signed right-shift entirely -- two's-complement
src/world.c:9:// negative values just become large unsigned ones, and unsigned arithmetic
src/world.c:10:// wraps predictably, which is all a hash needs.
src/world.c:11:static uint32_t mix32(uint32_t x) {
src/world.c:12:  x ^= x >> 16;
src/world.c:13:  x *= 0x7feb352dU;
src/world.c:14:  x ^= x >> 15;
src/world.c:15:  x *= 0x846ca68bU;
src/world.c:16:  x ^= x >> 16;
src/world.c:17:  return x;
src/world.c:18:}
src/world.c:19:
src/world.c:20:// Combines all three axes -- hashing fewer than three would collapse a
src/world.c:21:// whole vertical column (same x,z, varying y -- the common case when a
src/world.c:22:// player stands in one spot) into a single bucket. Each axis is mixed
src/world.c:23:// independently, then multiplied by a different large odd constant before
src/world.c:24:// XOR so the three don't cancel each other out on structured input (e.g.
src/world.c:25:// coords that differ only in one axis, which is most real chunk-load
src/world.c:26:// traffic).
src/world.c:27:static uint32_t world_hash(ChunkCoord coord, uint32_t capacity) {
src/world.c:28:  uint32_t h = mix32((uint32_t)coord.x) ^
src/world.c:29:               mix32((uint32_t)coord.y) * 0x9e3779b9U ^
src/world.c:30:               mix32((uint32_t)coord.z) * 0x85ebca6bU;
src/world.c:31:  // % works for any capacity; if you size world_init() with a power-of-two
src/world.c:32:  // capacity you can replace this with `h & (capacity - 1)` instead (no
src/world.c:33:  // division). Left as % for now since capacity isn't constrained to be a
src/world.c:34:  // power of two.
src/world.c:35:  return h % capacity;
src/world.c:36:}

src/world.c:83:bool world_insert(World *w, ChunkCoord coord, Mapblock block) {
src/world.c:84:  if (w->count >= w->capacity) {
src/world.c:85:    // Hard-fail, don't rehash-and-grow: capacity is sized once up front for
src/world.c:86:    // the largest view distance you intend to support. Running out means
src/world.c:87:    // that budget was wrong, not that this function should silently cover
src/world.c:88:    // for it.
src/world.c:89:    fprintf(stderr,
src/world.c:90:            "world_insert: table full (capacity %u) -- raise capacity, "
src/world.c:91:            "don't grow silently\n",
src/world.c:92:            w->capacity);
src/world.c:93:    exit(1);
src/world.c:94:  }
src/world.c:95:  uint32_t i = world_hash(coord, w->capacity);
src/world.c:96:  for (;;) {
src/world.c:97:    WorldSlot *slot = &w->slots[i];
src/world.c:98:    if (slot->state == SLOT_EMPTY) {
src/world.c:99:      slot->state = SLOT_OCCUPIED;
src/world.c:100:      slot->coord = coord;
src/world.c:101:      slot->block = block;
src/world.c:102:      w->count++;
src/world.c:103:      return true;
src/world.c:104:    }
src/world.c:105:    if (slot->state == SLOT_OCCUPIED && chunkcoord_equal(slot->coord, coord)) {
src/world.c:106:      // Overwrite: insert doubles as update for an already-loaded chunk
src/world.c:107:      // (e.g. re-decoding a mapblock the server resent). The old block's
src/world.c:108:      // heap allocation (if MAPBLOCK_FULL) is freed first so this doesn't
src/world.c:109:      // leak -- if you wanted "caller bug" semantics instead, this is
src/world.c:110:      // where you'd assert/hard-fail instead of destroying+replacing.
src/world.c:111:      mapblock_destroy(&slot->block);
src/world.c:112:      slot->block = block;
src/world.c:113:      return true;
src/world.c:114:    }
src/world.c:115:    i = (i + 1) % w->capacity;
src/world.c:116:    // No bounds check against a probe count here: the w->count >= capacity
src/world.c:117:    // check above guarantees at least one EMPTY slot exists before this
src/world.c:118:    // loop starts, so it's guaranteed to terminate.
src/world.c:119:  }

src/net.c:272:        return;

src/net.c:274:

src/net.c:283:            break;

src/net.c:306:        if (n <= 0)

src/sha256.c:27:        uint32_t s0 = rotr(w[i - 15], 7) ^ rotr(w[i - 15], 18) ^ (w[i - 15] >> 3);
src/sha256.c:28:        uint32_t s1 = rotr(w[i - 2], 17) ^ rotr(w[i - 2], 19) ^ (w[i - 2] >> 10);
src/sha256.c:29:        w[i] = w[i - 16] + s0 + w[i - 7] + s1;

src/sha256.c:41:        uint32_t temp2 = S0 + maj;
src/sha256.c:42:
src/sha256.c:43:        h = g; g = f; f = e; e = d + temp1;

src/sha256.c:45:    }
